question: A study group debates breadth-first and depth-first graph traversal. Which claim is accurate?
options: Both traversals visit nodes in the same order.
Breadth-first uses a stack and depth-first uses a queue.
Traversal order is identical on every graph.
Breadth-first explores level by level; depth-first goes deep first.
gold_answer: Breadth-first explores level by level; depth-first goes deep first.
notes: Team-authored original item on breadth-first and depth-first graph traversal. Passages are team-authored derivations recorded under sciclaim-appx-A. Requires independent annotation and adjudication before any gate result is reported.

positions.answer: Breadth-first uses a stack and depth-first uses a queue.

claims.text: Breadth-first finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

evidence.text: First discovery happens along a shortest route, since all nearer vertices are processed first.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage ties first discovery to shortest routes, which entails the claim.

claims.text: Traversal visits each edge at most zero times.

evidence.text: Systematic traversal examines each reachable edge at least once to find all reachable vertices.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage requires examining each edge, which refutes the claim.

claims.text: Graph algorithms are only useful for social networks.

evidence.text: Application domains were listed for the graph library.

claims.verdict_rationale: A listing cannot show exclusive usefulness, so the claim is neither established nor refuted.

positions.answer: Breadth-first explores level by level; depth-first goes deep first.

claims.text: Depth-first search uses a stack, explicitly or via recursion.

evidence.text: The last-discovered vertex is explored first, which is exactly stack discipline.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage identifies stack discipline, which entails the claim.

evidence.text: Queues release the oldest waiting vertex, producing breadth-first order rather than depth-first.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage assigns queues to breadth-first order, which refutes the claim.

evidence.text: Graph families were classified with trees as one special case.

claims.verdict_rationale: Calling trees a special case cannot show all graphs are trees, so the claim is neither established nor refuted.

positions.answer: Both traversals visit nodes in the same order.

claims.text: Breadth-first search expands vertices in order of distance.

evidence.text: The queue releases vertices level by level, so nearer vertices emerge before farther ones.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage describes level-by-level release, which entails the claim.

evidence.text: Deep excursions can discover far vertices through long routes, missing shorter ones.

claims.verdict_rationale: The passage describes missing shorter routes, which refutes the claim.

evidence.text: Downstream results were compared under two orderings.

claims.verdict_rationale: Comparing orderings cannot show order never matters, so the claim is neither established nor refuted.
